Status page

When a big service has a problem, millions of people open its status page to see what is happening. The page must stay up exactly when everything else is down, and it must not share a home with the thing it reports on. A few staff update it by hand. Practise this easy system design problem for free with a Google or GitHub account.

Play this problem

The brief

When a big service has a problem, millions of people open its status page to see what is happening. The page must stay up exactly when everything else is down, and it must not share a home with the thing it reports on. A few staff update it by hand.

Think of a public status page.

Users, scale and requirements

Who uses it
5 million visitors in a bad week (approx.)
Audience in plain numbers
5,000,000 users or devices
Normal peak
≈ 800 requests per second
Request mix
Read: 99%; Write: 0.5%; Sign-in: 0.5%
Speed for 99 of 100 requests
Read: ≈ 400 ms; Write: ≈ 400 ms; Sign-in: ≈ 1,000 ms
Successful requests
99.9%
Data safety
At most 1 minute of writes may be lost.
Monthly budget
≈ $3,500
Data at rest
≈ 0.01 TB
Where users are
North America: 50%; Europe: 30%; Asia Pacific: 20%
Home region
North America
Waiting deadlines
Read: 900 seconds; Write: 3,600 seconds; Sign-in: 900 seconds

≈ marks an approximation, just as in the game. Waiting deadlines measure the age of queued work and are separate from interactive response time.

  • The whole page is a few kilobytes of text (approx.).
  • During a big outage reads can be 5 times the usual (approx.).
  • All numbers are rough approximations.

Questions that shape the design

How fresh must the page be?

About 30 seconds behind is fine. Staff updates do not need to appear instantly.

Can it live next to the main service?

It should not. If the main region fails, the status page has to keep working.

How many people write to it?

A handful of staff. Almost all traffic is reading.

The traffic day

Fairly steady traffic throughout the day. The clock covers 00:00 to 24:00 in the home region. Events add pressure on top of that normal traffic.

  1. 14:00 · Flash crowd

    A scheduled launch brings a sudden rush of requests.

    Traffic reaches 5 times the scheduled load; rises over 30 seconds, holds for 900 seconds and eases over 1,800 seconds.

  2. 14:20 · Zone outage

    An availability zone loses power or network access.

    Duration: ≈ 3,600 seconds.

What a strong design has to handle

  • Everyone reads the same page. How many of those reads must reach your own servers?
  • A 30 second copy is slightly stale. Anything shorter costs more origin traffic with little gain.
  • Hosting away from the main service means a second set of accounts to look after, but it survives the failure you are reporting.

Make a prediction, run a full traffic day, then compare the result. The in-game editorial opens after a finished day and includes measured reference designs.

Concepts to practise

  • Surviving a region
  • Copies near users
  • SLOs and error budgets
  • The simplest thing that works

Related problems

  • Hard

    Metrics platform

    Thousands of services send a stream of measurements: CPU, errors, latency. You store them, draw the dashboards and fire the alerts. The platform watching everyone else must never go down first, and one customer creating millions of new series can ruin the bill.

  • Hard

    Maps and routing

    You run a maps app with places, routes and live traffic. Map pictures never change much, but route lookups, place search and traffic from moving phones do. Soon a whole new continent will start using it. Keep maps fast everywhere without paying to serve the same picture twice.

  • Medium

    Feature flag service

    Companies turn features on and off for groups of users without redeploying. Millions of apps ask "is this on for me?", and the answer must be instant. A wrong flag value can take down an entire customer, so changes must roll out safely and be reversible in seconds.

  • Hard

    Logs platform

    Build a shared log service for 2,000 teams. Collectors send compressed chunks, and on-call engineers find logs by tenant, service and time before filtering their words. A wide search or a runaway label must not stop other teams from investigating an outage.
